cases.title: `n` opens the create-task modal.
`/` focuses the search box.
`g` then `l` / `b` / `t` navigates to List, Board, Timeline.
`?` opens the keyboard shortcut reference.
`Esc` closes the topmost dismissible layer, one at a time.
`[` collapses and expands the sidebar.
`t` cycles the theme.
Shortcuts are suppressed while a modal or menu owns the keyboard.
The full list → open → edit → save → close cycle works with no mouse.
Filtering is fully keyboard-operable.
Creating a task is fully keyboard-operable end to end.
The sidebar is fully keyboard-navigable.
The header avatar menu is keyboard-operable per menu conventions.
Modals trap focus.
Focus returns to the trigger when a dialog closes.
A visible focus indicator is present on every focusable element, in both themes.
Focus survives async content replacement.
Focus moves into newly revealed content.
Tab order follows visual order.
Icon-only buttons expose accessible names.
Toggle controls expose their state, not just their label.
Every form field has a programmatically associated label.
Field errors are programmatically associated with their field.
Async outcomes are announced in a live region.
Filter result counts are announced when they change.
The task table uses real header semantics.
Sort state is exposed and announced.
Board drag-and-drop has a keyboard alternative.
Relationship reorder and timeline resize have keyboard alternatives.
Colour is never the sole carrier of meaning.
Unavailable controls are announced as unavailable, with a reason.
The schema banner is announced as a page-level status, not skipped.
`Esc` on a dirty modal confirms before discarding.
Nested layers unwind in the right order.
A toast appearing does not steal focus.
Undo is reachable by keyboard before the toast disappears.
`prefers-reduced-motion` suppresses the board's animated reflow.
Browser zoom to 200% keeps every primary flow usable.
Text-only zoom to 200% does not break layout.
Contrast holds in both light and dark themes.
A very long task title does not break table row semantics.
A task with 20 labels stays keyboard-navigable.
Keyboard shortcuts do not collide with browser or screen-reader shortcuts.
A skip link reaches the main content.
Route changes are announced.
A failed save is announced, not just coloured.
An empty result and a failed load are audibly different.
The uninitialized-tracker screen is announced correctly.
The crashed-migration screen is fully readable by screen reader.
A destructive confirmation defaults focus to the safe choice and states the blast radius.
Partial bulk-operation results are announced accurately.
The server-unreachable state is announced and persistent.
A query-syntax error is conveyed without relying on the highlight.
The error boundary's fallback is keyboard-operable.
A round-trip loses none of the seven things the CSV drops.
The backup carries values, and the CSV is untouched by it.
A malformed line is reported and skipped; nothing else is lost.
History is in by default and can be opted out
A binary attachment survives byte-for-byte.
The export reports its own size cost.
A tracker above the threshold splits and reconstructs.
A partial set is refused, not half-restored.
Bare restore refuses a non-empty tracker.
`--merge` adds absent ids and edits nothing else.
A key collision reallocates and the old key still resolves.
Key counters merge by max, so no key is ever reissued.
`--overwrite` replaces the ids it carries and says what it destroyed.
Restore is atomic at every kill point.
`--dry-run` predicts accurately and changes nothing, in all three modes.
Config restores with its values, so a bare machine works.
A name collision keeps both and renames the incoming one.
A reference that cannot be satisfied fails with the thing named.
The file streams — it is read without parsing the whole of it.
Colliding project prefixes are resolved, not left to double-issue keys.
A backup carries its schema version, and a mismatch is refused with both versions named.
Restoring into a tracker that is itself mid-operation refuses.
The four merge hazards, together.
Restore's merge is sync's merge, not a second implementation.
A row checkbox selects exactly one task and nothing else.
The bulk bar appears on the first selection and states the count.
Select-all in the header selects the visible page and says so.
"Select all N matching" is a separate, explicit action.
Bulk Set status applies the chosen status to every selected task.
Bulk Set priority uses configured priorities.
Bulk Set assignee excludes archived users from the picker.
Bulk Set milestone and Set sprint behave like Set assignee.
Move to project relocates every selected task and rekeys them.
Bulk Archive is immediate, undoable, and not gated behind a typed confirm.
Bulk Delete demands a typed confirmation scaled to the blast radius.
Confirmed bulk delete removes the tasks and reports honestly.
Clear selection (×) empties the selection without side effects.
Bulk actions the current workspace can't satisfy are hidden, not broken.
A filter change invalidates a selection rather than silently carrying it.
Paginating past the selected page keeps the count honest.
Sorting re-orders rows without dropping or corrupting the selection.
Shift-click selects a contiguous range.
A selected task deleted by another process is reported, not silently skipped.
A selected task edited by the CLI mid-selection reflects the new values after the bulk op.
Selecting every row of a 5,000-task filter via page selection stays responsive.
A bulk op spanning multiple projects works and states the spread.
Bulk Move to project across mixed source projects rekeys each task from the destination counter.
Bulk archive of tasks that are already archived is a no-op, reported as such.
Bulk assigning an archived user is refused before the write.
A status deleted from `workflow.yaml` between page load and apply is handled.
The delete confirmation names the actual scope, including a "select all matching" scope.
Bulk actions are disabled while one is in flight.
One bulk op produces one collapsible activity group per task.
Partial failure names every failure individually with its own reason.
Total failure is distinguished from partial failure.
A refused bulk op names the field, the value, and the fix.
A bulk request that never returns is bounded and honest about state.
A bulk op blocked by the state lock says which lock and what to do.
A failed delete leaves no half-deleted task.
A bulk move to a project that was archived mid-flight is refused with a reason.
Selecting more tasks than the API accepts in one request is handled before the request.
A network drop mid-bulk is reported with unknown-state honesty.
`/board` loads and renders one column per status when `workflow.boards` is absent.
Columns come from `workflow.boards.columns` when configured, collapsing multiple statuses into one column.
The status chips bar lists every visible column's statuses and toggles column visibility.
Chip visibility persists per user across reloads.
Cards render exactly the fields `UserSettings.card_layout` marks visible, in the stored order.
A column with a `wip` limit shows a count against the cap and flags going over.
An empty column shows a designed placeholder, not a blank strip.
Clicking a card opens that task's detail.
Dragging a card to a different column writes status and `board_rank` in one atomic call.
Dragging a card within its own column writes `board_rank` only.
Drop targets are visible during a drag and the reflow is animated.
A column collapsing several statuses does not rewrite a card's status on an intra-column reorder.
A card dropped into a multi-status column adopts the column's first status.
The board respects the shared filter bar and reflects filters in the URL.
Twenty statuses produce twenty columns that scroll horizontally rather than squashing.
One status produces one column, and it does not stretch to a full-width slab of cards.
A `boards.columns` entry naming a status that no longer exists in `workflow.yaml` renders the column and explains the gap.
A task whose `status` was deleted from `workflow.yaml` is visible, not vanished.
Two statuses whose labels are identical still resolve to distinct columns.
A status with an empty-string-ish or emoji label renders without breaking column layout.
A column holding 900 cards stays usable.
A card with 20 labels and a 300-character title does not break the column.
A board scoped to "All projects" shows the project on each card and does not mix key prefixes confusingly.
A status not listed in any configured column has its tasks accounted for.
Dropping at the top of a column generates a rank strictly below the current first card.
Dropping at the bottom of a column generates a rank strictly above the current last card.
Cards with no `board_rank` sort below ranked cards and can be dragged to acquire one.
A rank that grows past the 24-character threshold triggers a window rebalance without visually reordering anything.
Two cards that somehow carry identical `board_rank` values render in a stable, deterministic order and are separable by a drag.
A `board_rank` that is not a valid lexorank string is tolerated.
Dropping a card into the exact position it already occupies is a no-op.
A background refetch that lands mid-drag does not yank the dragged card.
A CLI `setField` on a visible task lands on the board without a manual reload.
Two browser tabs reordering the same column converge on one order, not a phantom one.
A card moved to another column by another surface while being dragged in this tab resolves without inventing a state.
Toggling a column off while a card in that column is mid-drag cancels cleanly.
Drag is initiated by an intentional gesture, not by a stray mouse-down.
A card can be moved between columns without a mouse.
The board has a designed loading state, not a flash of empty columns.
A tracker with zero tasks shows a board-level empty state, not six identical placeholders.
A cross-column drop that fails on the server snaps the card back and says why.
A drop into a column whose status was deleted from `workflow.yaml` since page load is rejected legibly.
Losing the connection mid-drop does not leave the card visually moved.
A drop onto a task that no longer exists fails with a specific message.
A malformed `workflow.boards` block does not blank the board.
One corrupt `task.md` does not take down the board.
A card-layout settings write that fails leaves the board rendering the last-known-good layout.
A chip-visibility write that fails is reported, and the discrepancy is visible.
A rebalance that fails partway leaves a consistent order, not a scrambled column.
Board cards surface "blocked" and "epic".
The board header status pills read as visibility toggles.
Workflow writes are validated before they land.
A task holding a drifted enum value is visible, marked, and findable.
Config values can be read back wherever they can be written.
Config error text matches the CLI's.
`loctt calendar` says what it cannot do.
Comments list oldest-first.
The composer posts a comment without leaving the page.
Comment bodies render markdown.
Edit and delete are offered on every comment, not only the current user's own.
Editing a comment marks it edited.
Deleting a comment confirms once and removes it.
@mention autocomplete filters as you type.
Archived users are excluded from NEW mentions.
Mentions render as chips.
Mentions survive a rename of the mentioned user.
Multiple mentions in one comment all resolve.
Editing a comment recomputes its mentions.
The activity feed is reverse-chronological and grouped by day.
Field changes show before and after values.
Each history kind has its own icon and phrasing.
Consecutive entries sharing a `bulk_op_id` collapse into one expandable row.
"Load more" pages through history without duplicating or skipping.
Comments and Activity are separate, addressable sections.
A task with no comments and no history shows designed empty states.
80 comments render without collapsing the page.
A comment mentioning a hard-deleted user still renders.
Markdown injection and script tags in a comment are neutralized.
A comment posted from another surface appears in the UI.
Editing a comment that was deleted elsewhere fails cleanly.
300 history entries collapsing into few bulk groups still paginate correctly.
A `field_change` referencing a since-deleted config value still renders.
A `custom_field_change` renders using the field's configured label and type.
An entry with no `actor` renders honestly.
Entries from a `key_history` rename resolve.
Timestamps within the same minute are ordered stably.
Day headings respect the calendar's first day of week and holidays only where relevant.
A failed comment post does not lose the text.
Posting with no current user is refused with a route out.
A delete that fails does not remove the comment from the list.
An edit of another user's comment succeeds and is attributed.
A corrupt comments file degrades the section, not the task.
A corrupt `_history.yaml` degrades the activity feed only.
A "Load more" failure keeps the loaded entries and offers retry.
A relationship activity entry reads with the relationship's human label and the correct article, never the raw config key.
The comment lifecycle is reachable from both surfaces.
Posting with no current user is refused with a route out.
A body write based on a stale read is refused.
Long histories are reachable past the newest page.
`loctt log` renders labels and display names, not raw keys and ULIDs.
Every mutating operation writes a history entry.
A corrupt history file is reported, not silently emptied.
`get_task_history` does not mutate core's returned array.
An object-fatal task is reported unreadable and attributed, and blocks nothing else.
A wrong-typed known field degrades to a health finding; the task still loads.
Editing one field preserves an untouched corrupt sibling byte-for-byte.
A valid write over a corrupt field repairs it; an unset removes it.
The write guard never introduces corruption and never silently drops it.
The operation rule: a read-to-compute refuses over a corrupt field; a read-for-idempotency repairs.
An unrecognised frontmatter key is preserved and surfaced, not dropped.
An untitled task shows its key, never a blank.
A corrupt config entry degrades to a broken marker; the rest of the file loads.
A structurally-broken config file refuses, attributed, without taking down unrelated surfaces.
"Broken" is distinct from "empty" and from "failed to load" on the surfaces.
state.yaml is object-fatal by necessity, with an attributed error.
A user profile degrades every field but `id`.
A dangling reference degrades to a marked value — never blank, never a full ULID.
A relationship edge distinguishes healthy / corrupt-but-present / corrupt-unreadable / genuinely-absent.
An invalid enum / workflow-drifted value keeps its raw key and is marked.
A corrupt-dated task is distinguished from an undated one on the timeline.
A malformed history/comment row is reported incomplete and kept in place; object-fatal blocks.
Backup/restore preserves dropped fields and never overwrites an unreadable destination.
The attachments section degrades independently of task health.
Reconcile marks a corrupt side of a conflict so it is not merged as empty.
A saved view referencing a dropped field/entity stays listed and runnable.
Health travels on the wire only when present, and never leaks the raw object.
A config write never drops a sibling entry it did not touch, broken or not.
Aggregates count a degraded task and name an unreadable one; a total is never silently short.
Publish gates on object-fatal corruption but proceeds through field-local corruption, reporting both.
Duplicate and merge over a corrupt task carry health correctly, not a raw corrupt value.
Settings drop a bad known key to default yet keep unknown passthrough keys; a load never overwrites an unreadable file.
A corrupt field renders with an inline warning on the task-detail page, not as an empty "—".
An unreadable label is shown and repairable in Settings → Labels, not omitted.
A global data-integrity indicator points users to Diagnostics.
Health travels through the CLI/MCP task shape only when present, and the raw object never leaks.
An untitled task shows its key on the CLI and MCP, never a blank.
A broken config entry is surfaced by `list`, never read as "none".
Repair and derived-op refusal reach the CLI/MCP as clear outcomes, not stack traces.
The CLI/MCP relationship display mirrors the four target states.
A workflow-drifted value keeps its raw key and is marked on both surfaces.
A malformed history/comment is reported incomplete through the CLI/MCP, not silently shortened.
A bulk op over a corrupt member reports it as failed-because-unreadable, not as "not found".
The server not running says the LocTT server is unreachable, and does not read as "no tasks".
The UI recovers on its own when the server comes back.
A request failing mid-write rolls the optimistic update back visibly and says the change was not saved.
A write whose outcome is genuinely unknown says so rather than guessing.
A very slow request shows progress, then a bounded, actionable timeout.
A 500 carrying a specific server reason shows that reason verbatim.
A 404 on a resource the UI thought existed names the resource and offers a way out.
A 404 from a hand-typed or stale URL is distinguishable from an app crash.
One malformed `task.md` does not take down the list.
A malformed config file names the file, the failing field, and what was expected.
A read-only or wrong-ownership `.loctt/` is named as a permission problem, ideally before work is lost.
Disk full names the cause and does not discard the user's typed content.
A bulk operation where some items fail states the split and names each failure.
Every error appears where the problem is, not only in a corner toast.
Recovery is offered as a control, not merely described.
No jargon leaks into user-facing copy.
Errors are dismissible and coalesce rather than stacking into a wall.
Every message that reports a failure also reports the data state.
A truncated or malformed response body is handled as a failure, not parsed into a broken UI.
A response with the right shape but nonsense values does not silently corrupt the view.
An empty error body from the server still produces a useful message.
A 400/422 from request validation is presented as a field problem, not a protocol problem.
A failure during a multi-step user flow says which step failed and what has already been applied.
An attachment upload failure does not leave a phantom attachment.
A bulk op that fails entirely says nothing was applied, distinctly from partial success.
A bulk op where every item fails for a different reason lists every reason.
An auto-save failure is as loud as a manual save failure.
An error state inside a sidebar group is contained to that group.
Two unrelated errors at once are both legible.
A genuinely unknown failure may say the cause is unknown — but must still answer three questions.
The unknown-cause wording is honest about being unknown, not vague to hide a known cause.
Audit: no routine failure lands in the generic handler.
The generic handler is reachable at all, and is tested.
A render crash is contained to a region where possible, not a white page.
The error boundary tells the user their data is on disk and unaffected.
The error boundary offers reload as a control and names what broke.
Crash detail is retrievable, just not in the headline.
An error in the error surface does not cascade.
No failure is silent.
No success is claimed for a failure.
An error state and an empty state are never the same rendering.
Error copy is written for the person running the tool, not for the developer who wrote it.
Errors about config values use the user's labels, not raw keys.
Error surfaces are keyboard-reachable and announced.
Error messages survive a route change without becoming misleading.
Enabling git-backed mode says what it will do first.
Publish reports what changed, not "OK".
Sync reports what it pulled in.
Status shows the last synced commit and drift indicators.
Auto-mergeable fields merge without opening the reconciliation panel.
The reconciliation panel lists conflicting fields with both sides.
Applying reconciliation writes the chosen values and completes the operation.
Rekeying prints a summary before applying.
ULID breaks a `created_at` tie during rekey.
Disabling git-backed mode says what it does and does not do.
The same custom field key changed to different values is a conflict, not a merge.
A conflict on 30 tasks at once.
`parent` conflicts are shown as tasks, not raw ULIDs.
A conflicting value references a status that no longer exists locally.
Publish with both sides changed runs reconciliation before the push.
One side deleted a task the other side edited.
All conflicts resolve to values identical on both sides.
Reconciliation was interrupted halfway and `local/reconcile.yaml` is still present.
A rekey affects a task the user has open in another tab.
The CLI publishes while the UI's panel is open.
The `loctt` branch was force-pushed and no longer contains the last synced commit.
The tracker lives on iCloud Drive or a network share.
A sync brings in 500 new tasks.
A publish that only touches gitignored files is a no-op.
Enabling git sync when a `loctt` branch already exists from a previous setup.
The reconciliation panel is a designed state, not a modal that loses work on navigation.
Git sync enabled on a repo with no remote.
The directory is not a git repository at all.
Publish fails because the push is rejected.
Sync fails because the remote is unreachable.
Publish reports success while reconciliation is still pending.
Apply fails partway through a 30-task reconciliation.
Rekey fails after the summary was confirmed.
The `loctt` branch contains files that fail schema validation.
The remote was written by a newer schema version.
The publish worktree is missing or corrupt.
A conflicting task file becomes unwritable during Apply.
Sync is triggered while a previous sync is still running.
Two edits to different fields of one task merge instead of conflicting.
Two clones creating tasks offline do not collide on keys.
An interrupted reconciliation is resumable.
A failed push is reported as a failure.
Git failures are named, not passed through raw.
Git status reports drift, not just configuration.
`loctt git enable` on a repo with an existing `loctt` branch is deliberate.
`enable_git`'s description matches what it does.
Enable on a non-git directory leaves nothing behind.
Every git operation honours a reconfigured `git.branch`.
`/` redirects to `/list` and lands on a populated table.
The table renders all ten columns with the user's configured vocabulary.
Clicking a column header sorts by it and writes the sort to the URL.
Sorting by a priority set with no `value` falls back to alphabetical.
Clicking a row opens that task's detail route.
Per-user column visibility and order come from `UserSettings.list_columns`.
A loading skeleton occupies the table while the first request is in flight.
A filter matching nothing shows a distinct empty state, not the fresh-tracker one.
Each filter dropdown offers the configured options and writes a typed search param.
Active filters render as removable chips that stay in sync with the URL.
Back and forward replay filter history step by step.
The "Show archived" toggle includes archived tasks and marks them.
Pagination reports an honest count and loads more in place.
A DSL query in the search box runs the same language as the CLI.
Query aliases and dotted fields resolve as documented.
The custom-field picker adds a filter for a declared field.
Filters, sort, and pagination compose into one shareable URL.
5,000 tasks with no filter stay responsive.
A task with 25 labels does not break the row.
A 400-character title with no spaces does not blow out the layout.
CJK, RTL, and emoji grapheme clusters render and sort sanely.
Dates at the far ends of the range render correctly.
Relative timestamps respect the workspace calendar timezone, not the browser's.
A status deleted from `workflow.yaml` while tasks still reference it degrades visibly.
An assignee referencing an archived user still resolves.
A task with no `project` in frontmatter is listed, not hidden.
Unknown priority and type keys are handled the same way as unknown statuses.
Unknown top-level frontmatter keys are ignored by the list without being lost.
An unknown sort key in the URL falls back visibly.
Out-of-range and malformed pagination params are clamped, not obeyed.
A truthy-looking `archived` param does not accidentally enable the toggle.
Unknown search params are preserved, not stripped.
A filter value referencing a deleted entity is honest about it.
Duplicate values in a CSV param are de-duplicated.
Filtering while a page-2 load is in flight does not mix result sets.
A task edited in the CLI while the list is open does not stay stale indefinitely.
A task deleted underneath the list disappears cleanly.
Two tabs hold independent list state.
A task created in the CLI appears in a matching filtered view.
A DSL query and structured filter chips compose predictably.
An empty search box clears the query without clearing the chips.
A query string containing quotes and escapes round-trips.
A query matching every task still paginates.
A malformed query reports the error instead of returning zero results.
An unknown field in a query names the field and what is valid.
A query referencing an undeclared custom field is distinguished from a typo'd built-in.
The API being unreachable is reported as such, distinctly from an empty tracker.
One corrupt task file does not take down the list.
A failed "Load more" does not look like the end of the list.
A server error while applying a filter does not leave a lying view.
A workflow config that fails schema validation is explained, not crashed on.
A request that times out is reported as a timeout, not as empty.
A free-query (`q=`) filter shows a chip and a Clear-all.
The first click on a priority (and due) sort header sorts the most-useful direction.
Sidebar links do not silently carry the ambient sort
Facet dropdown items show a multi-select affordance before the first click.
The Milestones view lists every non-archived milestone with its target date and progress bar.
Progress counts by status category, not by a `done` key.
Discarded-category tasks are handled by an explicit, stated rule.
Clicking a milestone opens its task list.
Labels render as coloured pills on both cards and rows.

Clicking a second label adds to the filter rather than replacing it.
Creating a label in Settings → Labels writes to `labels.yaml`.
Recolouring a label updates every surface that renders it.

A task carrying 20 labels does not break row or card layout.

`calendar.yaml` changing under a live session updates date rendering.
A config file legitimately empty of a category renders as empty, not broken.
`.schema-version` missing: the UI says the tracker is unrecognized and points at `loctt migrate`.
Recorded version greater than current: `SchemaTooNewError`, and migration cannot help.
Recorded version less than current: run `loctt migrate`.
The M4 "Migrate now" button runs the real migration and clears the banner.
The `.schema-migration-in-progress` sentinel blocks every boot and must not be one-click "fixed".
Schema state is re-evaluated, not cached from the first page load.
Tasks created out-of-band are found by key without a rebuild.
Tasks deleted out-of-band stop resolving cleanly.
A manual frontmatter edit to `key` or `key_history` is the one drift LocTT cannot auto-detect, and the UI must point at the CLI.
`key` and `key_history` are rejected as immutable by the web API, matching the CLI and MCP.
An old key still resolves after a sync collision rekeys the task.
Searching for a historical key finds the task.
Relationship links survive a rekey.
The detail footer shows key history so a changed bookmark is explicable.
The UI reports a state-lock timeout honestly rather than hanging or claiming success.
Writes during a migration fail fast, with the migration named as the reason.
A stale lock left by a killed process clears within its documented timeout.
The UI warns when the tracker sits on a filesystem where advisory locks are unsafe.
A malformed file the UI reads is a genuine hand-edit, never a torn write.
Machine-local files are not published and are not required to be present.
UI, CLI, and MCP all open on the same tracker stay coherent.
Two browser tabs on the same tracker behave like two separate surfaces.
Switching the current user in one surface is reflected in the others.
The UI never presents stale data as authoritative when it knows it is stale.
A write rejected because the underlying task changed says exactly that.
A task deleted in the CLI while the UI has it open degrades to an explicit not-found state.
A query the UI cannot parse fails at the offending token, not by returning zero rows.
A query referencing a config value that no longer exists is not silently empty.
A config file that fails its Zod schema names the file and the failing field.
`projects.yaml` violating its at-least-one-project constraint is reported specifically.
Duplicate project keys or prefixes are reported as the constraint violation they are.
A read-only or wrong-ownership `.loctt/` is detected before the user does work they will lose.
A conflict surface that itself fails still leaves the file untouched.
A saved view that the UI wrote but that fails to reload is reported as a write problem, not a missing feature.
